title: Behavioral Priming: Buy, Robot Human!
summary: Josh and Chuck explain priming, the psychological effect where exposure to a stimulus (a word, image, temperature, or metaphor) unconsciously shapes later responses. They cover cognitive priming examples (lexical decision, word-completion, repetition priming), fMRI evidence, and how marketing and media use agenda setting, framing, and priming. They then trace social priming studies from the late 1970s and John Bargh's elderly-walking study, the Ten Commandments and honesty-pledge experiments by Dan Ariely, and the Nobel-winning endorsements by Daniel Kahneman and Richard Thaler. The episode then turns critical: the replication crisis, p-hacking, fabricated data (Diederik Stapel), questionable research practices, and why social priming is now largely discredited, with only narrow, legitimate effects remaining. A listener mail segment about the Sea Monkeys episode closes the show.

entities.name: Nudge: Improving Decisions about Health, Wealth, and Happiness

segments.title: Opening banter and definition of priming
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and define priming as being prompted to respond or choose in a certain way based on an unnoticed stimulus.

segments.title: Explicit vs implicit memory and lexical decision
segments.summary: Explanation of explicit (conscious) and implicit (unconscious) memory, and the lexical decision task where a priming word such as doctor speeds recognition of related words such as nurse.

segments.title: Word completion and repetition priming
segments.summary: Examples of word-stem completion (soup versus soap) primed by surrounding words, and repetition priming where repeated pairs are recognized faster; fMRI studies show different brain regions activate under priming.

segments.title: Shift from cognitive to social priming
segments.summary: The hosts note that cognitive priming has real-world uses in marketing and advertising, setting up the move into social psychology and the nudge economics trend.

segments.title: Sponsor break and Burger King ad anecdote
segments.summary: A short break; Chuck jokes about repetitive Burger King commercials during TV reruns, illustrating repetition in advertising.

segments.title: Media and politics: agenda setting, framing, priming
segments.summary: The hosts describe how media and politicians use agenda setting, framing, and priming, using crime coverage as an example of shaping public fear.

segments.title: Dog whistling and implicit bias tests
segments.summary: Dog whistling is defined as coded language tied to implicit bias. The hosts discuss implicit bias tests, the response-time thresholds, and that people who reject stereotypes still show bias on these tests.

segments.title: Early social priming experiments: hostility and temperature
segments.summary: The 1979 scrambled-sentence hostility study (Donald and the landlord) and the warm versus cold beverage study by John Bargh shaped impressions of strangers.

segments.title: John Bargh elderly walking study and its collapse
segments.summary: Bargh's study in which students primed with elderly-related words walked more slowly down a hall; the hosts say it was ridiculed and that the field has been largely discredited.

segments.title: Questionable social priming findings
segments.summary: The hosts list dubious findings: fishy smells and trust, frowning and self-reported upset, money priming and selfishness, stabbing a coworker and buying cleaning products, and lying and mouthwash versus soap preference. They also discuss the power pose claim.

segments.title: Kahneman, Thaler, and Ariely endorsements of nudge priming
segments.summary: Daniel Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow insisted priming results were true; Thaler's Nudge promoted social priming; Dan Ariely's Ten Commandments and honesty pledge studies showed less cheating on tests and less mileage fudging.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the replication discussion.

segments.title: Replication crisis and Kahneman's open letter
segments.summary: Replication failures in psychology, especially social psychology; Kahneman's open letter to John Bargh warning of a train wreck; the Replicability Index blog by Ulrich Schimmack; and the hosts' view that the field's fame came from splashy results.

segments.title: Fraud, data massaging, and open science
segments.summary: Accusations against Dan Ariely and Francesca Gino over data massaging, the honesty pledge data mismatch, fabrication by Diederik Stapel, and open science measures such as preregistration to prevent HARKing.

segments.title: Why priming is unreliable and what remains legitimate
segments.summary: Humans are not predictable; results vary by person and experimenter; the Stanford prison experiment is cited. Legitimate priming works mainly when it points toward existing goals, such as dieting menu words. The hosts then discuss why the field was attractive, including the non-player character idea.

segments.title: Cheeseburger tangent
segments.summary: Lighthearted banter about cheeseburgers after the word was repeated throughout the episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sea Monkeys episode
segments.summary: Listener Katie Sesenler from Istanbul describes falling asleep during the Sea Monkeys episode and waking to discussion of white supremacists and the KKK, and thanks the hosts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminder of listener mail address and show credits.
